title: Build the Right Thing: Product Engineering (Part 2) — Kent C. Dodds, EpicProduct.engineer
talk_summary: Kent C. Dodds argues that once AI agents commoditize implementation, the differentiator is deciding what to build: dig past feature requests to a job-to-be-done statement, then prioritize with the Kano model (basics, performance, delighters, indifference, reverse). He explicitly warns against piping user requests straight into an agent that auto-implements them.

takeaways.what_they_do: Before any implementation, ask 'why' repeatedly until you can write a job statement (situation → progress → outcome → without X); refuse to design a system for a request that has no job attached.
Explicitly rejects the pattern of feeding user requests directly into an agent that implements them, because it produces a product with no vision or judgment.
takeaways.evidence_quote: takes the user's request and sends it into an agent and just automatically implements it. Stop.

takeaways.what_they_do: Classify each request as basic / performance / delighter / indifference / reverse, and set the engineering bar (reliability, reversibility, effort) per class rather than a flat priority list.
Treat features nobody cares about as maintenance dead weight and remove them rather than migrate/maintain them.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we spent two weeks maintaining this feature. Is anybody using that?

takeaways.what_they_do: Engineers are expected to push back on features users would hate (e.g., auto-posting to social media) instead of building them.
takeaways.evidence_quote: could you please push back on those stupid ideas that are like making our lives awful?

takeaways.what_they_do: Validate the problem with behavioral questions ('when did you last hit this, what did you do instead?') and a rough prototype before committing engineering effort.
takeaways.evidence_quote: when was the last time you experienced this pain and what did you do instead?
